questions.q: What is MySQL's two-argument NULL-coalescing function, equivalent to T-SQL's ISNULL?
options: IFNULL(expr, replacement)
NULLIF(expr, replacement)
NVL(expr, replacement)
ISNULL(expr, replacement) — identical spelling to T-SQL
questions.explain: IFNULL is MySQL's two-argument shortcut; the spelling differs from T-SQL's ISNULL even though the behavior matches.

questions.q: How does COALESCE differ from IFNULL in MySQL?
options: COALESCE takes any number of arguments and works identically across dialects; IFNULL is a MySQL-specific two-argument shortcut
COALESCE only works with numeric types, IFNULL only with strings
IFNULL is deprecated and COALESCE is its only replacement
COALESCE is MySQL-only and does not exist in T-SQL
questions.explain: COALESCE is the standard, portable function; IFNULL is MySQL's convenient but dialect-specific two-argument version of the same idea.

questions.q: What is MySQL's equivalent of T-SQL's STRING_AGG, and how does its separator syntax differ?
options: GROUP_CONCAT(expr SEPARATOR ', ') — the separator is a keyword inside the call, not a second comma-separated argument
CONCAT_AGG(expr, ', ') — syntax identical to STRING_AGG
MySQL has no equivalent function and requires a manual loop
JOIN_ROWS(expr, ', ')
questions.explain: GROUP_CONCAT uses the SEPARATOR keyword inside the function call, a small but real syntax difference from STRING_AGG's comma-separated second argument.

questions.q: How does MySQL quote an identifier that clashes with a reserved word, compared to T-SQL?
options: Backticks, e.g. `order` — where T-SQL uses square brackets, e.g. [Order]
Double quotes, identical to T-SQL
MySQL does not allow reserved words as identifiers under any syntax
Square brackets, identical to T-SQL
questions.explain: Backtick quoting is MySQL's identifier-quoting convention, distinct from T-SQL's square brackets.

questions.q: How does sql_mode relate to MySQL's historical implicit type conversion leniency?
options: Stricter sql_mode settings reduce some implicit coercion, moving behavior closer to T-SQL/Oracle/PostgreSQL
sql_mode has no effect on type conversion at all
sql_mode only controls character set conversion, not type coercion
Implicit type conversion is disabled entirely regardless of sql_mode
questions.explain: The leniency connects directly to Lesson 43's sql_mode discussion — stricter modes tighten some of MySQL's historically loose type coercion.
